extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners who design or evaluate rating/coding instruments (e.g., psychologists, survey researchers, clinical researchers, content analysts, measurement specialists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and summary of statistical methods and conceptual definitions for assessing agreement among multiple observers who rate, code, or assess the same phenomena. Covers operational definitions, behavior models, a range of agreement statistics (kappa, ICC, correlations, Bland–Altman, Krippendorff's alpha), and practical issues in training and scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that assessment tools exhibit good inter-rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment tools that rely on ratings must exhibit good inter-rater reliability, otherwise they are not valid tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-rater reliability is presented as a prerequisite for validity of rating-based assessment tools; designers and evaluators should ensure sufficient agreement among observers before treating scores as valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions of agreement (three definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three operational definitions of agreement: (1) reliable raters agree with the 'official' rating of a performance; (2) reliable raters agree with each other about the exact ratings to be awarded; (3) reliable raters agree about which performance is better and which is worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These differing definitions reflect distinct targets for reliability (concordance with a standard, exact-score agreement, or rank-order agreement) and imply different measurement and evaluation approaches depending on which notion is relevant to the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions of rater behavior (automatons vs independent witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two operational definitions of rater behavior: (a) reliable raters are automatons, behaving like 'rating machines' (e.g., computer grading); (b) reliable raters behave like independent witnesses and may disagree slightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behavioral models suggest different analytic frameworks: automaton-like behavior can be evaluated by generalizability theory, while independent-witness behavior can be evaluated by the Rasch model. Choose the model that matches expected rater behavior when selecting reliability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint probability of agreement (percent agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-probability of agreement is the simplest measure: estimated as the percentage of the time the raters agree in a nominal or categorical rating system. It does not take into account that agreement may occur by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution: when there are few categories (2–3), chance agreement increases and percent agreement can be misleadingly high. A useful coefficient should be near 0 with no intrinsic agreement and increase with intrinsic agreement; joint probability fails to correct for chance, so consider chance-corrected measures when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa statistics (Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa, extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa measures agreement correcting for chance. Cohen's kappa works for two raters; Fleiss' kappa adapts for any fixed number of raters. Original kappas treat data as nominal and ignore ordering; extensions handle partial credit and ordinal scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kappa is similar to a correlation (range −1 to +1) and commonly only positive values are expected. Kappa can only reach high values when agreement is good and the target condition's base rate is near 50% (because base rates factor into joint probabilities). Use ordinal/weighted kappas or other extensions when data are ordered; be aware of commonly cited 'rules of thumb' for interpreting magnitude but consult context-specific guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise correlation coefficients for ordered scales (Pearson, Kendall, Spearman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pearson's r, Kendall's τ, or Spearman's ρ can be used to measure pairwise correlation among raters when the scale is ordered. Pearson assumes a continuous rating scale; Kendall and Spearman assume only ordinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For more than two raters, compute the coefficient for each pair and take the mean of the pairwise values to obtain an overall group agreement estimate. Choose the coefficient consistent with scale assumptions (continuous vs ordinal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ICC is defined as 'the proportion of variance of an observation due to between-subject variability in the true scores'. It has several types and ranges (commonly 0.0 to 1.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC is useful for interval/ratio or treated-as-ordinal scales and improves on Pearson/Spearman by accounting for differences in ratings across items and the correlation between raters. A high ICC indicates little variation between raters' scores for each item. Select the appropriate ICC formulation (one-way, two-way, consistency vs absolute agreement) according to study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of agreement and Bland–Altman plot (bias and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate differences between each pair of two raters' observations; the mean difference is bias and the reference interval (mean ± 1.96×SD) are limits of agreement. The Bland–Altman plot graphs differences versus averages to reveal agreement patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when two raters and continuous scales are involved. The limits indicate how much random variation influences ratings; assess whether limits are practically narrow or wide. For sample sizes ≤60 consider alternative formulae (e.g., ±2s) or the most accurate formula using the t critical value and a finite-sample correction: mean ± t_{0.05,n−1} s sqrt(1 + 1/n). Bland–Altman plots can show whether agreement depends on the magnitude of the measured quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krippendorff's alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Krippendorff's alpha assesses agreement among observers categorizing or measuring values and generalizes several specialized coefficients. It accepts any number of observers and applies to nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio levels; it handles missing data and is corrected for small sample sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krippendorff's alpha is versatile across measurement levels and common in content analysis, counseling, survey coding, observational studies, psychometrics, and computational linguistics. Prefer it when datasets have missing values or variable numbers of coders per item and when a single, general reliability coefficient is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations and management of disagreement; need for clear scoring guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Raters are expected to disagree for tasks involving ambiguity; unambiguous measurement (e.g., simple counting) may not require multiple raters. Measurement tasks with ambiguous characteristics benefit from multiple trained raters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clearly stated scoring guidelines to reduce error variance from differing procedures and interpretations. Without scoring guidelines, ratings are prone to experimenter's bias and rater drift. Mitigate rater drift with periodic retraining and ensure raters understand guidelines and measurement goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing measures by measurement level and structure (items vs cases; nominal→ratio continuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different statistics are appropriate for different types of measurement and data structure: nominal (kappa-family), ordinal (ordinal kappa or ICC with careful assumptions), interval/ratio (ICC), and variants that analyze agreement across raters by items or raters-by-cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a reliability statistic that matches both the measurement level (nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio) and the study design (two raters vs many, fixed vs random rater sets, per-item vs per-case analysis). Consider extensions that handle partial credit, ordinal data, and aggregation across items as needed.
